resources.string: Upscaling factor (1.0 = native, 1.5 = 1.5x, 2.0 = 2x). Higher values require more performance.
RCAS sharpening strength. Higher values increase edge contrast.
Apply a light denoising pass before upscaling to reduce artifacts.
Strength of the denoising filter. Only applies when denoising is enabled.
Enable FSR 1 EASU upscaling. Disable for sharpening only.
AMD FidelityFX Boost: Combines FSR 1 upscaling (EASU), RCAS sharpening, and optional denoising for enhanced image quality.
How far the glow spreads from bright areas.
Strength of the glow added on top of the image.
Bleeds light out of the brightest areas into a soft halo, the way a camera does when pointed at something too bright.
How far the blur reaches, in pixels.
Blend between the original image and the blurred one.
Size of the region left in focus at the centre of the screen. At zero the whole image is blurred evenly.
How gradually the sharp centre gives way to the blur.
Gaussian blur with an optional sharp centre, for softening the picture or faking depth of field.
Speed of the rolling bar. Zero disables it.
Horizontal separation of the red and green channels.
Curved scanlines and the phosphor mask of a CRT television, for games that were drawn with that kind of screen in mind.
Darkness of the ink outline drawn around detected edges.
How many bands the colours are quantised into.
Ink outlines and flat colour bands. Faithful port of the PPSSPP shader; the outline gets heavy in dark scenes, so try Cartoon Soft or Cel Shading if the blacks smear.
Holds the outline back in dark areas. Raise it if shadows turn into black blobs.
How far the picture is pushed towards flat bands.
Ink outlines and flat colour bands, with the outline held back in the shadows so dark scenes do not turn into black blobs.
How many flat steps the lighting is collapsed into. Three or four gives the classic look.
Spreads the bands towards pure black and white. Lower it if the shadows crush.
Width of the transition between bands. Low values give hard cel steps.
How much surface texture survives the flattening. At zero the bands are completely flat.
Opacity of the ink line drawn along detected edges.
How strong an edge has to be before it is inked. Raise it to keep ink off textures and specular highlights.
Colour intensity of the flat regions.
Collapses the lighting into a few hard steps and inks the edges, keeping texture detail and hue intact.
Channel separation in pixels, measured at the edge of the screen.
How fast the separation grows away from the centre. Higher keeps the middle clean.
Splits the colour channels apart towards the edges of the screen, the way a cheap lens fails to focus every colour on the same spot.
The four basic colour controls in one pass: saturation, brightness, contrast and gamma. Reach for this before anything more specialised.
How flat a neighbourhood must be before it gets smoothed. Raise it to catch wider bands, lower it to keep more detail.
How far the sampling reaches, in pixels. Wider gradients need a larger radius.
Noise added to break up whatever banding survives the smoothing.
Smooths the visible steps in gradients such as skies, then dithers whatever survives. Worth adding whenever large flat areas show rings.
Edge preserving blur that clears dithering and compression noise while leaving outlines sharp. Ported from Anime4K.
Zero gives monochrome grain, one gives independent noise per channel.
Adds photographic grain, strongest in the midtones and fading out in blacks and whites.
Above 1.0 deepens the shadows, below 1.0 lifts them.
Above 1.0 opens up the highlights, below 1.0 compresses them.
Filmic contrast curve. Deepens the shadows and opens the highlights without clipping either end.
Positive bulges the picture outwards, negative pinches it inwards.
Scales the picture to hide the edges the warp pulls in.
Barrel or pincushion warp, like looking through a wide angle lens.
Input level mapped to black. Raise it to deepen washed out shadows.
Lifts crushed shadows so detail stops collapsing into one flat black.
Black point, white point, gamma and output range. Use it to fix crushed or washed out shadows.
How far the streaks reach, as a percentage of screen height.
Streaks running out from the centre of the screen, as if rushing forward. The centre stays sharp.
Streaks running in one fixed direction, as if the camera were sweeping across.
Direction of the sweep, in degrees.
Streaks curling around the centre, as if the camera were rolling. Negative turns the other way.
Camera style motion blur: streaks the picture outwards, sideways or around, without touching still detail at the centre.
Gamma applied to the luminance channel in YIQ space.
Boost applied to the two colour difference channels.
Warms the picture and lifts saturation for a less washed out look. Ported from the PPSSPP shader.
Height on screen where the reflective floor begins. Everything above it is left untouched.
How strongly the reflection shows through the floor.
How quickly the reflection fades as the floor comes towards the viewer. At zero it stays even.
Stretches or squashes the mirrored image. One is a true mirror, higher values pull it towards the line.
Amplitude of the waves disturbing the reflection. At zero the mirror is perfectly still.
Mirrors the picture into a reflective floor below a line you choose, with optional water ripples.
Number of scanline pairs across the screen.
How dark the gaps between lines become.
Strength of the green-warm phosphor cast.
Darkens alternating rows of pixels to imitate the horizontal scanlines of a CRT. Cheaper than the full CRT effect when you only want the lines.
Unsharp mask that brings back edge detail lost to scaling. Most useful after upscaling a low internal resolution.
Moves the split between what counts as shadow and what counts as highlight.
Tints the shadows and the highlights towards two different hues.
Darkens the corners of the screen to pull the eye towards the middle, the way a camera lens falls off at its edges.
Negative cools the picture towards blue, positive warms it towards orange.
Negative shifts towards green, positive towards magenta.
Corrects a picture that looks too cool, too warm or tinted.
Cel shaded look: the picture is cleaned first, then the lighting is collapsed into flat bands with inked edges, finished with a small glow.
Film look: soft glow on the highlights, a filmic contrast curve, cool shadows against warm highlights, fine grain and a gentle vignette.
Cleans up a low internal resolution: removes dithering and compression noise, smooths banded skies and brings edge detail back. The safe starting point if you are not sure what you want.
Soft focus: the centre of the screen stays sharp while everything around it blurs, with a wide glow over the highlights. Good for slower games and cutscenes.
Old television look: colour fringing at the edges of the screen, curved scanlines with a phosphor mask, and darkened corners. The scanline roll is switched off so it does not crawl.
Punchier colour without stylising the image: warmer and more saturated, blacks and whites pushed to the ends of the range, and a light sharpen.
